rationale: C04 plausibly supplied a material rhetorical template for the child statement: both frame increased military strength as simultaneously preparing for conflict and preventing it, then explicitly characterize that duality as paradoxical. The child compresses this same structure into the Polaris submarine's role as a devastating weapon conceived to preserve peace. C01 and C17 share the general contrast between destructive power and peaceful purposes, but neither matches the child's paradox-and-deterrence structure as closely.

shared_material.child_excerpt: our sea power, as are all elements of our national power, is a power for peace--a deterrent to any who would violate this eternal objective
shared_material.parent_excerpt: Our defense program, if carried through, will have the effect of discouraging aggression
shared_material.explanation: Both describe military strength as a deterrent that preserves peace.

shared_material.child_excerpt: The contradictions of Sam Houston are repeated in the paradox of the Polaris submarine.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: But paradoxical as it may seem, when the free nations have built up their forces, they may be able to convince potential aggressors that the control and reduction of armaments is a desirable policy.
shared_material.explanation: Both explicitly present the peace-producing function of military buildup as a paradox.

shared_material.child_excerpt: It is at once a devastating instrument of incredible destructive power, but at the same time it is conceived with but one purpose--to preserve the peace.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: Our present armament program, therefore, has a double purpose. It is above all an effort to prevent a world conflict, while at the same time it is an effort to prepare our defenses to meet such a conflict if it is forced upon us.
shared_material.explanation: The child closely adapts C04's two-sided formulation: weaponry prepares for destruction while serving chiefly to prevent conflict.
